🐛 Describe the bug
The signature of __getitem__ from the torch.nn.modules.container.ModuleList does not allow slice as the type for the variable idx, even though the code allows such type:
def __getitem__(self, idx: int) -> Union[Module, 'ModuleList']:
    if isinstance(idx, slice):
        return self.__class__(list(self._modules.values())[idx])
    else:
        return self._modules[self._get_abs_string_index(idx)]
As a consequence, type checkers like pyright (https://github.com/microsoft/pyright) will throw an error with the message:
Pyright: Argument of type "slice" cannot be assigned to parameter "idx" of type "int" in function "__getitem__"

A minimal example:
import torch.nn

module_list = torch.nn.ModuleList([torch.nn.Linear(2, 2) for _ in range(3)])
module_sublist = module_list[:-1]  # Pyright throws an error

In some cases we need to unfuse an operator like add_relu. To support aten:: ops that takes quantized inputs, we need to use the quantized_args decorator. In special aten:: cases, we also need to specify the requantization scale and zero points.
We would like to specify as little information about the op as possible when adding support for quantized args and infer as much info as possible.
Since there is a quantized tensor representation in TorchScript, we should be able to leverage that and avoid the need for explicitly specifying which arguments are quantized.
The proposed decorator will (1) register a symbolic function to a specified name and (2) apply specified transformations that alter the inputs
# Assuming the quantized::symbolic_a has signature 
# g, x: _C.Value, y: _C.Value, arg1: bool, op_scale, op_zero_point

@onnx_symbolic("quantized::symbolic_a", opset=10, decorate=[quantized_args_handler])
@symbolic_helper.parse_args("v", "v", "b")
def symbolic_a(g: _C.Graph, x: _C.Value, y: _C.Value, arg1: bool) -> _C.Value:
    ...
where default_quantization_handler turns any quantized input into de-quantized values, and re-quantizes the output with op_scale and op_zero_point.
This design allows for (1) easy discovery by simply searching for the op name (quantized::symbolic_a) to find the corresponding code (2) flexible code organization because the function does not need to live in a particular symbolic_opset file (3) function overloading by registering the same symbolic multiple times, or registering different symbolics that are design to handle the same aten op variations (4) flexible input transformation by providing a chain of decorators (5) easier code gen.
The proposed decorator also does not interfere with the current symbolic discovery process to allow for a gradual transition.
When we decide to use the register decorator for all ops, we will have
@onnx_symbolic("quantized::symbolic_a", opset=10, decorate=[quantized_op_handler])
@onnx_symbolic("aten::symbolic_a", opset=10)
@symbolic_helper.parse_args("v", "v", "b")
def symbolic_a(g: _C.Graph, x: _C.Value, y: _C.Value, arg1: bool) -> _C.Value:
    ...
When we need to specify zero_point and scale to an aten op, we can supply those to a handler e.g. quantized_args.
@onnx_symbolic("aten::symbolic_b", opset=10, decorate=[symbolic_helper.quantized_args(True, True, scale=1/128, zero_point=0)])
@symbolic_helper.parse_args("v", "v", "b")
def symbolic_b(g: _C.Graph, x: _C.Value, y: _C.Value, arg1: bool) -> _C.Value:
    ...
or more simply to a handler that will recognize quantized inputs e.g. quantized_aten_handler
@onnx_symbolic("aten::symbolic_b", opset=10, decorate=[quantized_aten_handler(scale=1/128, zero_point=0)])
@symbolic_helper.parse_args("v", "v", "b")
def symbolic_b(g: _C.Graph, x: _C.Value, y: _C.Value, arg1: bool) -> _C.Value:
    ...
to shorten what we need to type (if preferred), we can alias many things and do
register = functools.partial(onnx_symbolic, opset=10)

@register("aten::symbolic_a", decorate=[quantized_aten(1/128, 0)])
@symbolic_helper.parse_args("v", "v", "b")
def symbolic_b(g: _C.Graph, x: _C.Value, y: _C.Value, arg1: bool) -> _C.Value:
    ...

In benchmark/common.py, there is this timed function https://github.com/pytorch/torchdynamo/blob/b36e750dad8af509a003a386ddcbd2d0d331c983/benchmarks/common.py#L110-L119
, and this function is repeated for 30 times in a benchmark testing. This way of timing basically adds a cuda synchronization at every step.
The argument times is not used in function calls in speedup_experiment, so it's always the default value of 1. Should we add warmup and more iterations to it? For example,
def timed(model, model_iter_fn, example_inputs, bench_times=20, warmup_times=10, return_result=False):
    synchronize()
    torch.manual_seed(1337)
    # Dont collect outputs to correctly measure timing

    for _ in range(warmup_times):
        model_iter_fn(model, example_inputs, collect_outputs=False)

    synchronize()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()

    for _ in range(bench_times):
        result = model_iter_fn(model, example_inputs, collect_outputs=False)

    synchronize()
    t1 = time.perf_counter()

    time_ret = (t1 - t0) / bench_times

    return (time_ret, result) if return_result else time_ret
In a real example of pytorch_struct model, I can add a print statement here

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Situation
I am currently working on Evolutionary Strategies in PyTorch and I noticed that there is no efficient way to use Modules for defining a Network that I want to train. In EvoJAX it is possible to define flax Modules and vmap over their parameters and forward function. In PyTorch it is currently possible to vmap over forward functions, but not over parameters (at least not that I can think of any way).
Imagine following scenario
You want to train a simple MLP for solving XOR with Evolutionary Strategies in PyTorch.
Writing a custom forward method, this can be done very efficiently using einsums:
c: parameters of children in current population with shape [npop, params]
x: batched input: torch.tensor([[0., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 0.], [1., 1.]])
@torch.jit.script
def forward(c, x):
    # linear1 (in: 2, out: 2)
    x = torch.einsum('bi,nio->bno', x, c[..., :4].view(-1, 2, 2))
    x = x + c[..., 4:6]

    # relu
    x = F.relu(x)

    # linear2 (in: 2, out: 1)
    x = torch.einsum('bni,nio->bno', x, c[..., 6:8].view(-1, 2, 1))
    x = x + c[..., 8:9]

    return x
Now I would like to simply define my Network as nn.Module and  vmap over its parameters and forward function like this:
def f(model, c, x):
   torch.nn.utils.vector_to_parameters(c, model.parameters())
   return model(x)

outputs = vmap(f, in_dims=(None, 0, None))(model, child_params, X)
This is currently not possible, because parameter assignment is weird in PyTorch.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
For FSDP, one advantage of the FlatParameter is that registering a hook on its AccumulateGrad object gives us the correct time to schedule a reduce-scatter: The hook runs when all constituent original parameters' gradients are ready.
An alternative to this paradigm is to have a "multi-grad hook" that only runs once all passed-in tensors' gradients are ready. In that case, we can explore a new design for FSDP where we are not constrained to a single (large) flat_param.grad. Under such a new design, the FlatParameter would only be for communication and no longer relevant for autograd.
One effort this half is to provide an option to expose the original parameters in FSDP. The current approach manually sets .data to be views into the FlatParameter, and another approach is to use a tensor subclass like IndirectParameter. Regardless of the approach, as long as we have the FlatParameter interface with autograd and thus have its .grad attribute populated, we cannot save memory when only some of the original parameters require gradients. The parts of the .grad corresponding to parameters that do not require gradients will simply be zeros, but the entire .grad needs to be materialized.
This use case surfaces in finetuning, where there is a large model with only some small subset of parameters that require gradients and those parameters are spread throughout the module tree. PyTorch FSDP does not have good support for this at the moment. One option is to support a module having multiple FlatParameters, where we have the ones that do require gradient be in the same smaller FlatParameter and the ones that do not require gradient in another larger FlatParameter. This can work but is not ideal since it (unexpectedly) couples communication and autograd. The smaller FlatParameter will be less efficient to communicate.
Alternatives
The alternative is the current approach of having the FlatParameter interface with autograd.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
For FSDP, we want to run some unsharding logic before state_dict() runs for each module. With the existing FSDP design, FullyShardedDataParallel is a nested module wrapper, so we can override FullyShardedDataParallel.state_dict() to run the unsharding logic before calling super().state_dict(). However, in our effort to support FullyShardedDataParallel as a top-level-only wrapper, we want a state_dict() pre-hook to register on the original modules. This hook can run right before self. _save_to_state_dict():

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/modules/module.py
    
    
         Line 1436
      in
      bd0ad7a
    
  
  
    

        
          
           self._save_to_state_dict(destination, prefix, keep_vars) 
        
    
  


Alternatives
FSDP currently supports 3 model state dict options: full, local, and sharded. The precise differences are irrelevant. The idea to note is that sharded state dict employs a "trick": It lets super().state_dict() run normally without any preceding logic. Then, in the state_dict() post-hook, it runs the unsharding logic, saves the real entries to the state dict, and deletes the (sharded) entry populated by super().state_dict(). In that sense, it is only really using super().state_dict() for the prefix logic.
If FSDP a top-level-only wrapper, we follow a similar approach, only moving the state_dict() post-hook to the original modules. However, deleting the actual entries populated by state_dict() seems error prone. It may not compose well with other hooks.

        _tmp1 = tl.where(xmask & rmask, _tmp1 + tmp0, _tmp1)
    tmp1 = tl.reshape(tl.sum(_tmp1, 1), [XBLOCK, 1])
    tmp2 = tmp1
    _tmp8 = tl.zeros([XBLOCK, RBLOCK], tl.float32) + 0
    for roffset in range(0, rnumel, RBLOCK):

        tmp7 = tmp6 * tmp6
        _tmp8 = tl.where(xmask & rmask, _tmp8 + tmp7, _tmp8)
    tmp8 = tl.reshape(tl.sum(_tmp8, 1), [XBLOCK, 1])

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
CUDA graph is awesome for static graphs such as classification in CV, it greatly improves CNN's speed!
Currently I'm using CUDA graph on a big CNN model with 1k+ layers, batch size is 64. Activations in every layer is 64M level. I can train this model with activation checkpoint, but it will OOM when paring with CUDA graph, I find it's because every callable cuda graph will statically allocate 4 variables: input, output, grad output, grad input. This will cause huge memory consumption.
Can we find some way to reuse these statically allocated buffers?

When using with activation checkpointing, we can reuse CUDA graph's input with activation checkpointing input.
In FWD pass, grad output and grad input should be reused.
In BWD pass, when using with DDP, grad output and grad input can be reused when grad's allreduce finished

nodes.bodyText:
We use the Triton autotuner here:
https://github.com/pytorch/torchdynamo/blob/8e4abe3f66fb6b8d97d6461d64f9c3be323a523e/torchinductor/triton_ops/autotune.py#L182
and, here:
https://github.com/pytorch/torchdynamo/blob/8e4abe3f66fb6b8d97d6461d64f9c3be323a523e/torchinductor/triton_ops/autotune.py#L216
To select tile sizes for generated kernels from a short list of options.
This results in good performance, but has a high cost in terms of warm up time.  We will be running nearly identical autotuning runs to pick tilings that should be obvious.
I'd propose we create a small cost model to replace the autotuner.  As an input to this model we should take:

The size_hints (already rounded up to next power of two)
The indexing formulas of all the reads and writes
[Maybe] Number of tmpX variables used in kernel
[Maybe] Number of reduction loops in the kernel
[Maybe] Histogram of ops.* usage in the kernel

As an initial implementation, we could just build an on-disk cache/hash-table that runs the Triton autotuner on misses, but reuses a prior decision if the model inputs are identical.  This alone should dramatically speed up warmup times.
Longer term, we could take the data collected in this cache and train a small neural network to predict which tiling to use.  For this we should have the neural network predict the normalized runtime for each tiling choice.  This cost model can then replace the measurement step of the autotuner.

Incident timeline (all times pacific)

Aug 14th: PyTorch flaky test bot disabled a bunch of tests, i.e. (test_aot_autograd_exhaustive in TestEagerFusionOpInfoCPU) on this date. This probably tipped over the env variable length limit.
Aug 15th 9AM: OSS CI oncall was notified about the issue. There were also multiple alerts fired about trunk breakage.
Aug 15th 10AM: The fix was reviewed #83426 and force merged into master to facilitate the fix. Other can now rebase to get it and re-run the Windows tests.
Aug 15th 11AM: A minor update to the previous fix #83436

User impact
All Windows tests failed
Root cause
Windows env variable has an upper limit of 32767 characters, and we unknowingly used an env variable to keep the list of flaky (disabled) tests so that we can refer to it from time to time. Once there were too many flaky tests (262), this step failed on Windows
Mitigation

#83426 to not keep the list of flaky (disabled) tests in an env variable on Windows. Instead, we will just load the JSON structure directly from the file. This might has a tiny perf impact on running the tests, but that should be ok
Create a following up issue (#83458) to double check if:

It impacts other platforms (Linux, Mac, etc)
There's a better way to handle this, i.e. without using env variable, use multiple env variables, hashing, etc..



Prevention/followups

Find a better way to pass flaky (disabled) tests information around.  Loading it from file might not be that bad (if the file is small enough) #83458
Keep track of the number of flaky tests using Rockset query. I'll create a TTS metric for this
